newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Mitsubishi Motors Australia net loss widens in 96.
newsitem.headline: Mitsubishi Motors Australia net loss widens in 96.

text.p: Mitsubishi Motors Australia Ltd (MMAL) on Thursday reported a net loss of A$65.8 million for calendar 1996, compared to a net loss of A$43 million in 1995, but the company said it anticipated a much better performance in 1997.
Mitsubishi managing director Mike Quinn said strong competition within the Australian market had led to discounting and significant price repositioning.
MMAL is wholly-owned by Mitsubishi Motors Corp.

"This, coupled with the launch costs of the new models, Magna, Lancer, Mirage, Verada and Triton, and the start-up of our major export program to the United States, hampered profitability," Quinn said in a statement.
He said Mitsubishi's market share had lifted by the end of the year with all the new models in place.
"As a result we anticipate we will deliver a much better performance in 1997," he said.
Mitsubishi said 1996 sales revenue rose to A$2.06 billion from A$1.8 billion in 1995.
Total domestic registrations for its vehicles in 1996 were 61,079 units, resulting in a market share of 9.4 percent.
A further 11,967 units were exported to the United States, Japan, New Zealand and other countries in the Asia Pacific region, it said.
Exports were planned to rise to 19,000 units in 1997, it said.
Quinn said export volumes were allowing Mitsubishi to improve its manufacturing competitiveness.

But a strong domestic market was still needed to sustain a viable automotive industry in Australia, where the new car market had not risen significantly for three decades and was coming under pressure from imports, Quinn said.

The current review of the automotive industry by the Productivity Commission and the government's final policy decisions on industry assistance arrangements beyond 2001, due to be announced mid-1997, would be key factors for setting the future direction of carmaking in Australia, he said.
The Commission has proposed dramatic cuts in Australia's automotive tariffs, which carmakers have said could spell the end of the local industry.
